facts.statement: Aigialosuchus lived during the Early Campanian stage.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Campanian

facts.statement: The only species, A. villandensis, was described in 1959 by Per Ove Persson from fossils found in the Kristianstad Basin in southern Sweden.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, A. villandensis, described in 1959 by Per Ove Persson based on material recovered from the Kristianstad Basin in southern Sweden.

facts.statement: The precise classification of Aigialosuchus remains uncertain due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil remains.
facts.quote: The fragmentary nature of these remains means that the precise classification of the genus remains uncertain.

facts.statement: Since 2016, Aigialosuchus has been repeatedly classified within the basal family Dyrosauridae rather than as a eusuchian.
facts.quote: Though typically classified as an eusuchian, since 2016 it has been repeatedly placed within the more basal family Dyrosauridae.

facts.statement: During the Cretaceous, the Ivö Klack site where most Aigialosuchus fossils were found was a small, rocky island in a shallow sea covering southern Scandinavia.
facts.quote: In the Cretaceous, southern Scandinavia was covered by shallow sea and the Ivö Klack site within the Kristianstad Basin, where most of the fossils referred to Aigialosuchus have been found, was a small and rocky island.

facts.statement: Aigialosuchus likely fed on large fish and invertebrates, an adaptation suggested by its short, stout teeth.
facts.quote: Its teeth were short and stout, possibly an adaptation towards feeding on large fish and invertebrates.

facts.statement: Swedish paleontologist Per-Ove Persson described Aigialosuchus in 1959 based on fossils from the Ivö Klack locality in the Kristianstad Basin.
facts.quote: Aigialosuchus was described by Swedish paleontologist Per-Ove Persson in 1959 based on fossil material recovered at the Ivö Klack locality in the Kristianstad Basin.

facts.statement: Persson identified the main distinguishing feature of Aigialosuchus as the nasal bone extending to the fenestra exonarina communis.
facts.quote: Persson considered this material to be enough to clearly differentiate the fossil animal from all other known long-snouted crocodylomorphs, noting that the main distinguishing feature was the nasal bone of Aigialosuchus extending to the fenestra exonarina communis

facts.statement: A single blunt, wide tooth from Faxe, Denmark, might belong to Aigialosuchus or an alligatoroid genus.
facts.quote: A single, rather blunt and wide crocodylomorph tooth from the Faxe quarry in the Middle Danian-aged Faxe Formation at Faxe, Denmark, might be referrable to either Aigialosuchus or to some genus within the Alligatoroidea.

facts.statement: Aigialosuchus had a long and narrow snout.
facts.quote: Aigialosaurus was a long- and narrow-snouted crocodylomorph.

facts.statement: The nasal bones extended forward to the margin of the fused nostril opening, serving as the main diagnostic feature of the genus.
facts.quote: The nasal bones on both sides of the skull extended forwards until reaching the margin of this skull opening, this being the main diagnostic feature of the genus.

facts.statement: The mandibular symphysis of Aigialosuchus was unusually long at 13.8 centimetres (5.4 inches) and reached by the splenial bone.
facts.quote: Another diagnostic feature is the mandibular symphysis (the connection between the left and right mandible) of Aigialosuchus being unusually long, 13.8 centimetres (5.4 inches), and being reached by the splenial bone.

facts.statement: The broadened part of the skull was 7.1 centimetres (2.8 inches) wide at its widest point and 4.7 centimetres (1.85 inches) wide at the notches.
facts.quote: The widest portion of the broadened part is 7.1 centimetres (2.8 inches) wide and the width at the point of the notches is just 4.7 centimetres (1.85 inches).

facts.statement: Unlike modern crocodylians with long, slender teeth, Aigialosuchus had stout and short teeth.
facts.quote: In contrast to modern crocodylians, which typically have long and slender teeth, the teeth of Aigialosuchus were stout and short.

facts.statement: The teeth of Aigialosuchus were somewhat recurved and had cylindrical roots.
facts.quote: The teeth were also somewhat recurved and had cylindrical roots.

facts.statement: The surface of Aigialosuchus teeth was densely striated with ridges from base to tip.
facts.quote: The surface of the teeth was striated (covered in ridges) densely from the base to the tip.

facts.statement: Persson originally classified Aigialosuchus as a true crocodile within the subfamily Crocodylinae.
facts.quote: Persson classified Aigialosuchus as a true crocodile, placing it within the subfamily Crocodylinae.

facts.statement: In 2001, Christopher Brochu suggested Aigialosuchus was probably a eusuchian, the group containing all living crocodilians.
facts.quote: In 2001, American paleontologist Christopher Brochu noted that Aigialosuchus was an enigmatic crocodyliform, but probably a eusuchian (the group that contains all living crocodilians).

facts.statement: Elisabeth Einarsson classified Aigialosuchus as a dyrosaurid in a 2018 paper.
facts.quote: Aigialosuchus was also classified as a dyrosaurid in a 2018 paper by Swedish paleontologist Elisabeth Einarsson.

facts.statement: Fossils of Aigialosuchus have only been recovered from Campanian-age deposits in the Kristianstad Basin in Sweden.
facts.quote: Certain fossils of Aigialosuchus have only been recovered from the Campanian-age deposits in the Kristianstad Basin in Sweden.

facts.statement: The presence of Aigialosuchus at Ivö Klack suggests it may have preferred coastal waters to lay eggs on adjacent land and bask, similar to modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: The presence of Aigialosuchus at the site might indicate that Aigialosuchus preferred to live in coastal waters, where it could lay its eggs on adjacent land, rest and heat up, similar to modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: Einarsson suggested Aigialosuchus fed on various fish, ammonites, belemnites, and benthic macroinvertebrates based on its robust teeth.
facts.quote: According to Einarsson, the robust teeth of Aigialosuchus indicate that it was adapted for feeding on fish (such as lepisosteids, Protosphyraena, ichthyodectids, Pachyrhizodus, Enchodus, Cederstroemia, carcharhiniforms, and synechodontiformes), ammonites, belemnites, and benthic macroinvertebrates.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the precise classification of Aigialosuchus is certain due to fragmentary remains.
facts.quote: The fragmentary nature of these remains means that the precise classification of the genus remains uncertain.

facts.statement: Researchers note that the precise systematic position of Aigialosuchus within Crocodylomorpha remains unclear until a taxonomic revision is performed.
facts.quote: Schwarz-Wings, Milàn and Gravesen noted that until a taxonomic revision of the Aigialosuchus material is carried out, its precise systematic position within the entire Crocodylomorpha will remain unclear.
